title: Atoms, the Periodic Table and Bonding
bigQuestion: How can the structure of atoms, which no one can see, predict how the materials around us behave?

story.title: The Gaps Mendeleev Left on Purpose
story.kicker: In 1869 a Russian chemist arranged the known elements in a table and left empty boxes. Then he described what would fill them.
paragraphs: Dmitri Mendeleev was writing a chemistry textbook in St. Petersburg, and he had a problem. About 63 elements were known in 1869, and he needed some order to teach them in. He wrote each element's name and atomic weight on a card and dealt them out like a game of solitaire. When he lined the cards up by weight, something odd happened. Elements with similar behavior kept landing in the same column.

Lithium, sodium and potassium all react violently with water. In his rows they stacked up together. Fluorine, chlorine and bromine all form salts with those metals. They stacked up too. The pattern repeated every so often, like a song that returns to its chorus. Mendeleev called it periodic, from the word for a repeating cycle.

But the pattern had holes. If he trusted the columns, some boxes had to stay empty. Below aluminum there was a gap. Below silicon there was another. A cautious person might have hidden the gaps. Mendeleev did the opposite. He wrote down what the missing elements should weigh, what their density should be, and what kinds of compounds they should form.

For the element under silicon, which he called eka-silicon, he predicted an atomic weight near 72 and a density of about 5.5 grams per cubic centimeter. In 1886 a German chemist, Clemens Winkler, found a new element in a silver ore. He named it germanium. Its atomic weight was about 72.6. Its density was about 5.35. The gap had a name, and the prediction had come within a few percent.

Gallium filled the gap under aluminum in 1875. Scandium filled another in 1879. Each discovery turned Mendeleev's table from a tidy chart into a scientific tool: a pattern that could predict what no one had yet measured. This chapter asks where that pattern comes from. The answer lies inside the atom.
story.think: Mendeleev could have hidden the gaps in his table. Why was leaving them empty, and predicting what would fill them, a stronger scientific move?

lessons.title: Three Particles, One Atom
lessons.mainIdea: Every atom is built from protons and neutrons in a tiny nucleus, with electrons around it, and the number of protons decides which element it is.
reading: Take a pinch of salt and imagine cutting one grain in half, then in half again, over and over. Eventually you reach a piece that cannot be split without turning into something else. That piece is an *atom*. Atoms are astonishingly small. A single drop of water holds more of them than there are stars in the Milky Way. Yet each one has parts, and those parts follow rules.

In the center sits the *nucleus*, a dense knot made of two kinds of particles. *Protons* carry a positive electric charge. *Neutrons* carry no charge at all. Nearly all of an atom's mass is packed into this nucleus, but it takes up almost none of the atom's space. If the atom were a football stadium, the nucleus would be a marble on the fifty-yard line.

Around the nucleus move the *electrons*. Each has a negative charge exactly equal and opposite to a proton's, and a mass about 1,800 times smaller. In a neutral atom the number of electrons matches the number of protons, so the charges cancel. Electrons are what touch when two atoms meet, so they control almost everything about how an element behaves.

The one number that names an element is its proton count, the atomic number. Every atom with 6 protons is carbon. Every atom with 8 is oxygen. Change the proton count and you change the element itself. Change the number of neutrons or electrons and you still have the same element, just a different version of it.

words.d: the smallest piece of an element that still has that element's properties
the tiny, dense center of an atom, made of protons and neutrons
a positively charged particle in the nucleus; the number of protons names the element
a particle in the nucleus with no electric charge
a very light, negatively charged particle that moves around the nucleus

look.title: Rutherford's Surprise
look.text: Rutherford later described the result of firing alpha particles at thin gold foil in 1909. He said it was the most incredible event of his life, almost as if he had fired a large artillery shell at a sheet of tissue paper and it had bounced back and hit him. A few particles came straight back, which meant the atom had a tiny, heavy, charged center.
look.cite: Ernest Rutherford, recalling the gold-foil experiment, lecture given in 1936
look.prompt: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil. What does that tell you about how much of an atom is empty space?

check.q: Which particle count decides which element an atom is?
check.why: The atomic number is the number of protons. Every atom with 6 protons is carbon, no matter how many neutrons or electrons it has.

check.q: Where is almost all of an atom's mass found?
choices: In the empty space between particles
check.why: Protons and neutrons are far heavier than electrons, and they sit together in the nucleus.

check.q: A neutral atom has 11 protons. How many electrons does it have?
check.why: In a neutral atom the negative electrons exactly balance the positive protons, so there are 11 of each.

lessons.title: Isotopes: Same Element, Different Mass
lessons.mainIdea: Atoms of one element can have different numbers of neutrons; these versions are isotopes, and some of them are unstable.
reading: Every carbon atom has 6 protons. But if you could weigh carbon atoms one at a time, you would find that they do not all weigh the same. Most have 6 neutrons. About one in a hundred has 7. A tiny fraction, roughly one in a trillion, has 8. These versions are *isotopes* of carbon. They are the same element, with the same chemistry, but a different mass.

Scientists name an isotope by its *mass number*, the protons and neutrons added together. Carbon with 6 protons and 6 neutrons is carbon-12. With 8 neutrons it is carbon-14. The atomic mass printed on a periodic table is an average of all the isotopes, weighted by how common each one is. That is why carbon's listed mass is 12.011 rather than a whole number.

Some isotopes are stable and will sit unchanged forever. Others have a nucleus that is unbalanced, with too many or too few neutrons to hold together. These *radioactive* isotopes eventually change, shooting out a particle or a burst of energy. Carbon-14 is one of them. Its slow, steady decay is the clock used to date ancient wood and bone, which you will meet in the next chapter.

Isotopes matter in daily life more than most people realize. Doctors use a short-lived isotope of technetium to make images of the heart and bones. Smoke detectors in most homes contain a speck of americium-241. Water made with the heavy hydrogen isotope, deuterium, is used in some nuclear reactors. Same element, different neutron count, very different job.

words.d: an atom of an element with a particular number of neutrons; isotopes of one element differ in mass but not in chemistry
the number of protons plus neutrons in one nucleus
describes a nucleus that is unstable and will change by giving off particles or energy

look.title: Three Isotopes of Carbon
look.prompt: Carbon-14 is so rare it rounds to 0 percent. Why is the average atomic mass of carbon still slightly above 12?

check.q: Two atoms are isotopes of the same element. What must be different between them?
check.why: Isotopes share a proton count, which fixes the element, but have different neutron counts.

check.q: An atom has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. What is its mass number?
check.why: Mass number is protons plus neutrons: 6 + 8 = 14. This is carbon-14.

check.q: Why is chlorine's atomic mass listed as 35.45 instead of a whole number?
choices: Chlorine atoms are slightly bigger than others
It is an average of chlorine's isotopes, weighted by how common each is
Some of the mass is stored in the electrons
Scientists have not measured it carefully yet
check.why: Natural chlorine is a mix of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37, so its average mass falls between the two.

lessons.title: Electrons in Shells
lessons.mainIdea: Electrons fill energy levels around the nucleus in order, and the electrons in the outermost level, the valence electrons, control how an atom bonds.
reading: Electrons do not orbit the nucleus like planets. They occupy fuzzy regions called *energy levels* or shells, and each shell holds only so many. The first shell, closest to the nucleus, holds 2 electrons. The second holds 8. The third holds 8 before the next shell starts to fill. Electrons take the lowest open spot first, the way water fills a glass from the bottom.

Sodium has 11 electrons. Two fill the first shell, eight fill the second, and one lone electron sits in the third. Chlorine has 17: two, then eight, then seven. Neon has 10: two and eight, with the outer shell exactly full. These outermost electrons are the *valence electrons*, and they are the ones that meet other atoms.

Here is the key pattern. Atoms with a full outer shell, like neon and argon, are stable and almost never react. Atoms with one or two electrons more than a full shell tend to give them away. Atoms one or two short of a full shell tend to take or share. Sodium wants to lose one. Chlorine wants to gain one. That is why they combine so eagerly to form salt.

Chemists draw this with a simple sketch: the element's symbol surrounded by dots, one for each valence electron. Sodium gets one dot. Chlorine gets seven. Oxygen gets six. The sketch is a model, not a photograph, but it predicts an enormous amount of chemistry from a handful of dots.

words.d: a region around the nucleus where electrons can be found; each level holds a set number of electrons
an electron in the outermost energy level; valence electrons take part in bonding
unlikely to change or react; an atom with a full outer shell is stable

look.title: The Two Dots on Magnesium
look.text: Magnesium has 12 electrons: 2 in the first shell, 8 in the second, and 2 in the third. Oxygen has 8 electrons: 2 in the first shell and 6 in the second. Sketch both with dots for their valence electrons. Magnesium is 2 over a full shell. Oxygen is 2 short of one.
look.prompt: Predict what happens when magnesium and oxygen meet. Which atom gives, which takes, and how many electrons move?

check.q: How many valence electrons does chlorine (17 electrons) have?
check.why: Chlorine fills 2, then 8, leaving 7 in its outer shell.

check.q: Why do neon and argon almost never react?
choices: They are too heavy to move
check.why: A full outer shell is stable, so these atoms have no reason to gain, lose or share electrons.

check.q: Sodium has one valence electron. Based on the shell pattern, what is it most likely to do in a reaction?
choices: Gain seven electrons to fill its shell
check.why: Losing one electron leaves sodium with a full outer shell, which is the easiest path to stability.

lessons.title: Reading the Table
lessons.mainIdea: The periodic table lists elements in order of atomic number, and its rows and columns show repeating patterns that come from electron shells.
reading: Mendeleev ordered his elements by atomic weight, and it mostly worked. In 1913 a young English physicist, Henry Moseley, used X-rays to show that the true order was by atomic number, the proton count. A few elements that had seemed out of place snapped into position. The modern *periodic table* runs from hydrogen, with 1 proton, to elements with more than 100.

Each horizontal row is a *period*. Moving across a period, one proton and one electron are added at a time, and a new shell begins with each new row. Each vertical column is a *group* or family. Every element in a group has the same number of valence electrons. That is why they behave alike. Lithium, sodium and potassium each have one valence electron, and each reacts hard with water.

The table has neighborhoods. The far-left column, group 1, holds the alkali metals, soft and violently reactive. The column just before the right edge, group 17, holds the halogens, which grab electrons. The far-right column holds the noble gases, which barely react at all. The wide block in the middle holds the transition metals, including iron, copper and gold.

Metals sit on the left and center and make up most of the table. Nonmetals cluster in the upper right. A staircase of elements between them, such as silicon and germanium, are metalloids with a mix of properties. Germanium, the element Mendeleev predicted, sits on that staircase, which is exactly why it later became useful in electronics.

words.d: the chart of all elements arranged by atomic number so that elements with similar behavior line up in columns
a horizontal row of the periodic table; each row starts a new electron shell
a vertical column of the periodic table; elements in a group share a number of valence electrons
an element with some properties of metals and some of nonmetals, such as silicon

look.title: Mendeleev States the Law
look.text: In his 1869 paper Mendeleev wrote, in effect, that when the elements are arranged by their atomic weights, their properties show a clear periodic pattern. He added that elements whose atomic weights were still uncertain could be corrected by the pattern, and that new elements not yet discovered should be expected, such as ones resembling aluminum and silicon.
look.cite: Dmitri Mendeleev, paper read to the Russian Chemical Society, 1869
look.prompt: Mendeleev used the pattern to correct measured weights that did not fit. When is it reasonable for a scientist to trust a pattern over a measurement?

check.q: What does a vertical column, or group, on the periodic table tell you about its elements?
choices: They have the same number of valence electrons
They were discovered in the same year
check.why: Elements in a group share a valence electron count, which is why they behave alike.

check.q: What did Moseley's X-ray work change about the table?
choices: It showed the order should follow atomic number, not atomic weight
It proved Mendeleev's gaps were errors
check.why: Moseley showed the proton count sets the order, which fixed the few elements that had seemed misplaced.

check.q: Potassium is in group 1 with sodium. What should you predict about potassium and water?
choices: Potassium will not react, like argon
Potassium will dissolve quietly like salt
Potassium will react hard, like sodium
check.why: Same group, same valence electron count, same kind of behavior: group 1 metals react vigorously with water.

lessons.title: Why Reactivity Rises and Falls
lessons.mainIdea: Reactivity follows the table: metals react more going down a group, nonmetals react more going up, and the noble gases sit out.
reading: Drop a small piece of lithium in water and it fizzes. Sodium fizzes harder and can burst into flame. Potassium ignites almost at once. Rubidium and cesium react explosively. Going down group 1, each element has its one valence electron in a shell farther from the nucleus. That electron is held more loosely, so it leaves more easily. Looser electron, faster reaction.

The halogens in group 17 run the other way. Fluorine, at the top, is the most reactive nonmetal known; it attacks glass and most metals. Chlorine is a little tamer, bromine tamer still, iodine the mildest. Each wants one more electron to fill its shell. The smaller the atom, the closer that empty spot is to the pulling nucleus, so the top of the group grabs hardest.

This is *reactivity*: how readily an element takes part in a chemical change. It is not a random property. It comes from how tightly the nucleus holds its outer electrons, and that depends on the atom's size and the number of protons pulling. Chemists use the term *electronegativity* for an atom's pull on shared electrons. Fluorine has the highest value; the metals at the lower left have the lowest.

The noble gases in group 18 anchor the far right. Helium, neon and argon have full outer shells and almost no tendency to gain or lose anything. That is why helium fills balloons safely while hydrogen, which looks similar, once filled airships that burned. Knowing where an element sits tells you a great deal about how carefully to handle it.

words.d: how readily an element takes part in a chemical change
a measure of how strongly an atom pulls shared electrons toward itself
an element in group 17, such as fluorine or chlorine, that needs one electron to fill its outer shell
an element in group 18, such as neon or argon, with a full outer shell and very low reactivity

look.title: Two Unknown Metals
look.text: A lab has two unlabeled group 1 metals in oil. A tiny shaving of metal A fizzes gently in water. A shaving of metal B the same size bursts into a purple flame the instant it touches the surface. The teacher says one is lithium and one is potassium.
look.prompt: Which is which, and what about the size of the atoms explains the difference?

check.q: Going down group 1 from lithium to cesium, reactivity with water:
check.why: The valence electron sits farther from the nucleus in larger atoms, so it is lost more easily.

check.q: Which element pulls shared electrons most strongly?
check.why: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity: a small atom with a strong nuclear pull and one empty spot in its shell.

check.q: Why is helium safe in a balloon while hydrogen is a fire risk?
choices: Helium has a full outer shell and does not react
check.why: Helium is a noble gas with a full shell. Hydrogen readily reacts with oxygen and burns.

lessons.title: Size and Ionization Energy
lessons.mainIdea: Atoms get larger going down a group and smaller across a period, and the energy needed to remove an electron follows the opposite trend.
reading: You might expect an atom with more protons and electrons to be bigger. Across a period, the opposite happens. Lithium is larger than beryllium, which is larger than boron, and so on to neon. Each added proton pulls harder on the same shell, tightening the atom. Down a group, atoms do grow, because each new period adds a whole new shell farther out. Cesium is one of the largest atoms; helium is among the smallest.

*Ionization energy* is the energy it takes to pull one electron completely off an atom. Think of it as the price of stealing an electron. Sodium's price is low, about 496 kilojoules per mole, because its lone outer electron is far out and shielded by inner shells. Neon's price is high, over 2,000 kilojoules per mole, because its shell is full and close in.

The trend is a mirror of atomic size. Small atoms with many protons guard their electrons fiercely; large atoms with few outer electrons let them go cheaply. So ionization energy rises across a period and falls down a group. Fluorine and neon in the upper right are the hardest to ionize. Cesium in the lower left is the easiest.

These trends are why the table can predict behavior. A chemist who has never handled francium can still say with confidence that it is a very large atom, gives up its electron easily, and would react ferociously. Mendeleev predicted the densities and compounds of missing elements by exactly this kind of reasoning.

words.d: a measure of the size of an atom, from the nucleus to the outer edge of its electron cloud
the energy needed to remove one electron from an atom
the way inner electrons block part of the nucleus's pull on the outer electrons

look.title: First Ionization Energy Down Group 1
look.prompt: The numbers drop steadily down the group. Connect this to how the reactivity of these metals with water changes.

check.q: Moving across a period from left to right, atomic size:
choices: Increases, because more electrons are added
Decreases, because more protons pull on the same shell
check.why: The added protons tighten their grip on the same shell, so atoms shrink across a period.

check.q: Which element should have the lowest first ionization energy?
check.why: Cesium is large, with one outer electron far from the nucleus and heavily shielded, so it is easy to remove.

check.q: Why does sodium have a lower ionization energy than neon?
choices: Sodium's outer electron is in a new, farther shell and is shielded by the inner ones
check.why: Sodium's lone electron sits in the third shell, far from the nucleus and behind ten shielding electrons.

lessons.title: Ionic Bonds: Give and Take
lessons.mainIdea: When a metal gives electrons to a nonmetal, the resulting charged ions attract each other and lock into a crystal; that attraction is an ionic bond.
reading: Put sodium metal and chlorine gas together and they react with a flash, producing a white solid: ordinary table salt. Sodium's lone valence electron jumps to chlorine, which had room for exactly one more. Now sodium has a full outer shell but one fewer electron than protons, so it carries a positive charge. Chlorine has gained one and carries a negative charge. Charged atoms are called *ions*.

Opposite charges attract. The positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions pull toward each other from every direction and settle into a repeating three-dimensional pattern, a *crystal lattice*. Each sodium ion is surrounded by six chloride ions, and each chloride by six sodium ions. This electrical attraction holding the lattice together is an *ionic bond*.

Ionic compounds share a set of traits that follow from the lattice. They are hard and brittle: hit a salt crystal and it shatters along flat planes as like charges are shoved next to each other. They have high melting points, because every ion is held by many neighbors. Solid, they do not conduct electricity, since the ions cannot move. Melted or dissolved in water, they conduct well, because the ions are free.

Ionic bonds form between elements from opposite sides of the table: a metal with low ionization energy and a nonmetal with high electronegativity. Magnesium gives two electrons to oxygen to make magnesium oxide. Calcium gives two, one each, to two chlorine atoms to make calcium chloride, one of the salts spread on Chicago sidewalks before a snowstorm.

words.d: an atom or group of atoms that has gained or lost electrons and so carries an electric charge
the attraction between positive and negative ions that holds an ionic compound together
a repeating three-dimensional arrangement of ions or atoms in a solid
breaks or shatters rather than bends when struck

look.title: Two White Powders
look.text: A student has two unlabeled white powders. One is table salt (sodium chloride). One is sugar. She dissolves a spoonful of each in separate cups of water and tests each solution with a simple circuit and bulb. The bulb lights for one cup and stays dark for the other.
look.prompt: Which cup lit the bulb, and what does that reveal about the kind of particles each powder releases in water?

check.q: When sodium gives an electron to chlorine, what charge does the sodium ion carry?
check.why: Losing a negative electron leaves sodium with one more proton than electrons, so it is positive.

check.q: Why does solid salt not conduct electricity while salt water does?
choices: The ions are locked in place in the solid but free to move in solution
Salt is not made of charged particles
Solid salt has no ions until it melts
check.why: Conduction needs moving charges. In the lattice the ions are fixed; in water they move freely.

check.q: Which pair is most likely to form an ionic bond?
check.why: A group 1 metal that gives an electron easily and a halogen that takes one make a classic ionic pair.

lessons.title: Covalent Bonds: Sharing
lessons.mainIdea: Two nonmetals reach full shells by sharing electron pairs; the shared pair is a covalent bond, and it builds molecules.
reading: Two hydrogen atoms each have one electron and each want two. Neither can take from the other, because they pull equally. So they share. The two electrons spend their time between both nuclei, attracted to both, and hold the pair of atoms together. This shared pair is a *covalent bond*. The unit it makes, H2, is a *molecule*: a definite group of atoms bonded together.

Oxygen needs two more electrons, so it shares two pairs with another oxygen, a double bond. Nitrogen needs three and forms a triple bond, one of the strongest in chemistry. Water is one oxygen sharing a pair with each of two hydrogens. Methane, the main part of natural gas, is one carbon sharing a pair with each of four hydrogens. Chemists draw each shared pair as a short line between symbols.

Covalent bonds join nonmetals, which sit on the right side of the table. Because molecules are separate units rather than an endless lattice, covalent substances often have low melting points, and many are gases or liquids at room temperature. Water, carbon dioxide, oxygen and sugar are all covalent. They generally do not conduct electricity, since there are no free ions.

Sharing is not always equal. In water, oxygen pulls the shared electrons harder than hydrogen does, so the oxygen end of the molecule is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends slightly positive. This lopsided sharing is called *polar*. It is why water molecules cling to each other, why water has such a high boiling point for its size, and why it dissolves salt so well.

words.d: a bond in which two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons
a definite group of atoms held together by covalent bonds
describes a molecule or bond where electrons are shared unequally, giving one end a slight negative charge

look.title: Melting Points: Ionic Versus Covalent
look.prompt: What does the gap between the two groups of numbers tell you about the forces that must be overcome to melt each kind of substance?

check.q: What holds two hydrogen atoms together in an H2 molecule?
choices: A shared pair of electrons attracted to both nuclei
One atom's electron moving permanently to the other
The attraction between two positive nuclei
check.why: Neither atom can take the other's electron, so they share, and the shared pair is pulled by both nuclei.

check.q: Which substance is most likely covalent?
choices: A hard solid that melts above 800 °C
A gas made of two nonmetal atoms
A solid that conducts when melted
check.why: Nonmetals share electrons to form molecules, and small molecules are often gases at room temperature.

check.q: Why is water called a polar molecule?
choices: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons harder than hydrogen, so one end is slightly negative
Its atoms are arranged in a straight line
check.why: Unequal sharing gives the oxygen end a slight negative charge and the hydrogen ends a slight positive charge.

lessons.title: Metallic Bonds: A Sea of Electrons
lessons.mainIdea: In a metal, the atoms' outer electrons roam freely through the whole solid, which explains why metals conduct, bend and shine.
reading: Copper wire carries electricity to every outlet in a building. Aluminum foil bends around a sandwich without cracking. A polished spoon reflects your face. Ionic and covalent bonds cannot explain any of this. Metals bond a third way. Their outer electrons are held so loosely that they leave their atoms altogether and drift through the entire piece of metal.

Picture a grid of positive metal ions sitting in a shared pool of moving electrons. The ions attract the electron pool, and the pool attracts the ions, so the whole solid holds together. This is a *metallic bond*. No single electron belongs to any single atom. Chemists call the pool a sea of electrons, and the picture explains three properties at once.

First, *conductivity*. Because the electrons are already free to move, a small push from a battery sends them flowing as an electric current. They also carry heat quickly, which is why a metal spoon in hot soup warms fast. Second, *malleability*. Hammer a metal and the ion layers slide past each other while the electron sea flows around them, so the metal bends instead of shattering like salt. Third, luster: the free electrons absorb and re-emit light, giving metals their shine.

Alloys are metals mixed with other elements to tune these properties. Steel is iron with a little carbon, whose atoms jam the sliding layers and make the metal stronger. Brass is copper and zinc. Bronze, the metal of ancient tools and statues, is copper mixed with tin. Same electron sea, but foreign atoms in the grid change how easily the layers slide.

words.d: the attraction between positive metal ions and the free electrons that move among them
how well a material lets electricity or heat pass through it
the ability of a material to be hammered or bent into a new shape without breaking
a metal mixed with one or more other elements, such as steel or brass

look.title: The Bent Fork and the Broken Crystal
look.text: Two objects are struck with a hammer on the lab bench. A steel fork bends into a curve and stays bent. A large crystal of rock salt cracks into flat-sided pieces. Both were solids with strong bonds. Both were hit with roughly the same force.
look.prompt: Using the sea-of-electrons model and the ionic lattice model, explain why one bent and the other shattered.

check.q: In the metallic bonding model, where are the outer electrons?
choices: Moving freely throughout the whole metal
check.why: The sea-of-electrons model has valence electrons drifting through the entire piece of metal.

check.q: Why does copper conduct electricity so well?
choices: Its electrons are already free to move, so a push from a battery makes a current
It contains many ions in a lattice
check.why: Free electrons in the metallic sea flow easily when a voltage pushes them.

check.q: Why does adding carbon to iron make steel harder than pure iron?
choices: The carbon atoms jam the metal layers so they cannot slide as easily
Carbon forms ionic bonds with iron
Carbon makes the iron atoms larger
check.why: Foreign atoms in the grid interfere with the sliding of ion layers, making the alloy stronger.

lessons.title: Naming What You Make
lessons.mainIdea: Chemical names and formulas follow simple rules that tell you which atoms are present and in what ratio.
reading: A *chemical formula* is a recipe written in symbols. H2O means two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen. CO2 means one carbon and two oxygens. NaCl means sodium and chlorine in a one-to-one ratio. The small numbers after a symbol count that atom; no number means one. The formula does not show how the atoms are arranged, but it fixes exactly what is inside.

Ionic compounds are named metal first, nonmetal second, with the nonmetal's ending changed to -ide. Sodium and chlorine make sodium chloride. Magnesium and oxygen make magnesium oxide. The formula follows from the charges: the total positive charge must cancel the total negative. Magnesium ions are 2+, chloride ions are 1-, so it takes two chlorides for each magnesium: MgCl2.

Covalent compounds between two nonmetals use prefixes to count atoms, because the same pair can bond in more than one ratio. Carbon and oxygen make both carbon monoxide, CO, a poisonous gas, and carbon dioxide, CO2, the gas you breathe out. Mono- means one, di- means two, tri- means three, tetra- means four. Dinitrogen tetroxide is N2O4. The prefix mono- is dropped on the first element.

Some groups of atoms travel together as a charged unit, a *polyatomic ion*. Sulfate is SO4 with a 2- charge; nitrate is NO3 with a 1- charge; ammonium is NH4 with a 1+ charge. They are named as a unit: sodium sulfate, calcium nitrate, ammonium chloride. Fertilizer bags on Illinois farms list exactly these names, because the names tell a farmer precisely which ions the soil will receive.

words.d: a set of symbols and numbers that tells which atoms are in a substance and in what ratio
a group of atoms bonded together that carries an overall charge and acts as one unit
the small number after a symbol in a formula that counts atoms of that element

look.title: The Label on the Bag
look.text: A bag of garden fertilizer lists ammonium nitrate and potassium chloride among its contents. A student knows that ammonium is NH4 with a 1+ charge, nitrate is NO3 with a 1- charge, potassium ions are 1+, and chloride ions are 1-.
look.prompt: Write the formula for each compound. Then explain how the charges tell you the ratio without any prefix.

check.q: What does the formula CO2 tell you?
choices: One carbon atom bonded to two oxygen atoms
Two carbon atoms and one oxygen
Carbon and oxygen in any ratio
check.why: The subscript 2 counts oxygen atoms; carbon with no number means one.

check.q: Aluminum ions are 3+ and chloride ions are 1-. What is the formula for aluminum chloride?
check.why: It takes three 1- chlorides to cancel one 3+ aluminum, giving AlCl3.

check.q: Why do covalent compounds like CO and CO2 need prefixes in their names, while NaCl does not?
choices: Prefixes are only used for poisonous gases
Two nonmetals can combine in more than one ratio, so the name must count the atoms
check.why: Ionic ratios are fixed by charge, but nonmetals can share in several ratios, so the prefix tells them apart.

lessons.title: Why Salt Dissolves and Diamond Is Hard
lessons.mainIdea: A material's properties come from how its particles are bonded and arranged: the same element, bonded differently, can be soft or the hardest substance known.
reading: Stir salt into water and it vanishes. Stir sand into water and it sinks. Both are hard, white-ish crystals. The difference is what water can do to their bonds. Water molecules are polar, with a slightly negative oxygen end and slightly positive hydrogen ends. When water meets a salt crystal, the negative ends crowd around the positive sodium ions, and the positive ends crowd around the chloride ions. The ions are tugged loose one by one. Salt *dissolves*.

Sand is silicon dioxide, a covalent network in which every silicon is bonded to four oxygens and every oxygen to two silicons, on and on through the whole grain. There are no separate ions for water to pull away, and the covalent bonds are far too strong for water to break. So sand stays sand. Oil will not dissolve salt either, because oil molecules are not polar and cannot surround an ion.

Carbon shows most clearly that structure decides properties. In graphite, the soft gray material in a pencil, each carbon bonds to three neighbors in flat sheets. The sheets slide over each other easily, which is why pencils leave marks. In *diamond*, each carbon bonds to four neighbors in a rigid three-dimensional network. To scratch a diamond you must break covalent bonds, so diamond is the hardest natural material. Same element, different bonding, opposite behavior.

This is the payoff of the whole chapter. Metals conduct because their electrons roam. Salts shatter and dissolve because they are lattices of ions. Molecular substances melt easily because the molecules are only weakly attracted to each other. Network solids like diamond and quartz are hard because bonds run through the whole crystal. If you know the bonding, you can predict the behavior, and if you know the behavior, you can reason back to the bonding.

words.d: to break apart into particles that spread evenly through a liquid
a solid in which covalent bonds link atoms continuously through the whole crystal, such as diamond or quartz
a form of carbon in which each atom bonds to four others in a rigid three-dimensional network
a soft form of carbon made of flat sheets that slide over one another

look.title: Hardness on Mohs' Scale
look.text: In 1812 the German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs ranked ten minerals by which could scratch which. Talc was 1, the softest; gypsum 2; calcite 3; fluorite 4; apatite 5; feldspar 6; quartz 7; topaz 8; corundum 9; and diamond 10, which scratched every other mineral and could be scratched by none.
look.cite: Friedrich Mohs, mineral hardness scale, 1812; U.S. Geological Survey summary
look.prompt: Quartz is a covalent network like diamond, yet it rates 7 rather than 10. What besides bond type might explain the difference?

check.q: Why does salt dissolve in water but not in oil?
choices: Water is polar and can surround and pull apart the ions; oil is not polar
check.why: Polar water molecules attract each ion and tug it loose; nonpolar oil molecules cannot.

check.q: Graphite and diamond are both pure carbon. Why is one soft and the other extremely hard?
choices: Diamond has more protons per atom
In diamond every carbon is bonded to four others in a rigid network; in graphite sheets slide apart
check.why: Bonding arrangement, not the element, sets the hardness. Diamond's 3-D covalent network resists scratching.

check.q: A solid has a very high melting point, does not conduct electricity even when melted, and is extremely hard. Which type is it most likely?
check.why: No free charges even when melted rules out ionic and metallic; very high melting and hardness rule out small molecules. A network solid like quartz fits.

review.q: What did the discovery of germanium in 1886 do for Mendeleev's periodic table?
choices: It confirmed a prediction the table had made, showing the pattern could forecast unknown elements
It changed the order to atomic number
review.why: Germanium matched the properties Mendeleev predicted for eka-silicon, turning the table into a predictive tool.

review.q: An atom has 17 protons, 18 neutrons and 17 electrons. Which statement is true?
choices: It is chlorine-35 with a positive charge
It is argon with no charge
It is chlorine-35 and electrically neutral
review.why: 17 protons makes it chlorine; 17 + 18 = 35 is the mass number; equal protons and electrons make it neutral.

review.q: Which trend is correct across a period from left to right?
choices: Atoms get larger and ionization energy falls
Atoms get larger and ionization energy rises
Atoms get smaller and ionization energy falls
Atoms get smaller and ionization energy rises
review.why: More protons pull on the same shell, so atoms shrink and their electrons are harder to remove.

review.q: Which best explains why elements in the same group behave alike?
choices: They have the same number of valence electrons
They are all in the same state at room temperature
review.why: Valence electrons control bonding, and a group shares the same count of them.

review.q: A shiny solid bends without breaking and conducts electricity as a solid. What kind of bonding does it have?
review.why: Free electrons in a metallic bond give conduction, luster and malleability.

review.q: Which pair would most likely form a covalent bond?
review.why: Two nonmetals share electrons rather than transferring them.

review.q: Calcium ions are 2+ and nitrate ions (NO3) are 1-. What is the formula for calcium nitrate?
review.why: Two 1- nitrates are needed to cancel one 2+ calcium, so the polyatomic ion is written twice.

review.q: A crystal shatters when struck, melts at 800 °C, and conducts only when dissolved. Which explanation fits?
choices: It is an ionic lattice whose ions are fixed in the solid but free in solution
It is a metal with a rigid electron sea
It is made of small polar molecules
It is a covalent network like diamond
review.why: Brittleness, high melting point and conduction only when the ions can move are the signature of an ionic compound.
